output.abstract_summary: This paper introduces GEPA (Genetic-Pareto), a novel prompt optimizer that uses natural language reflection to learn high-level rules from trial and error. The authors argue that the interpretable nature of language provides a richer learning medium for LLMs compared to sparse scalar rewards used in RL methods like GRPO. GEPA works by sampling trajectories, reflecting on them in natural language to diagnose problems, proposing and testing prompt updates, and combining lessons from the Pareto frontier of attempts. The method achieves significant improvements across six tasks, outperforming GRPO by 6% on average (up to 20%) while using 35x fewer rollouts, and exceeding the leading prompt optimizer MIPROv2 by over 10% (including +12% on AIME-2025).

output.description: A flowchart of the GEPA optimization loop. It initializes a candidate pool, repeatedly samples candidates using Pareto-based filtering, proposes a new candidate through reflective prompt mutation or system-aware merge, evaluates it first on a minibatch and then on all tasks if performance improves, and either adds it to the pool or discards it until the budget is exhausted.
findings: The figure depicts iterative candidate improvement under a finite budget.
New candidates are generated using either reflective prompt mutation or system-aware merge.
Candidate selection uses task-wise best candidates followed by Pareto-frontier filtering rather than always mutating only the globally best candidate.
Each proposed candidate is evaluated on a minibatch before possible evaluation on all tasks.
Candidates that improve performance are added to the pool; candidates that do not improve are discarded.
The pool and scores matrix support maintaining multiple candidates with complementary task performance, promoting diversity and reducing local-optimum risk.

output.description: Figure 3 shows an iterative GEPA candidate-generation and evaluation workflow. A candidate pool is scored across tasks, Pareto-based filtering selects diverse high-performing candidates, and either Reflective Prompt Mutation or System Aware Merge proposes a new candidate. The candidate is evaluated on a minibatch; improved candidates are evaluated on all tasks and added to the pool, while non-improved candidates are discarded, within a while-budget loop.
findings: The figure depicts two candidate-generation strategies: Reflective Prompt Mutation and System Aware Merge.
P_new is first subjected to “Perform Minibatch Eval.”
The “Performance improved?” decision sends non-improved candidates to “Discard P_new.”
Improved candidates are evaluated on all tasks and added to the pool.
Candidate selection uses a “Scores Matrix,” “Best candidate per task,” and a “Filtered Pool (Pareto Frontier).”
The workflow is controlled by a “While Budget > 0” loop.
